items.title: Lauded social worker urges new approach to improve 'alarming' NT job vacancies
paras: Kylie Stothers says a "one-size-fits-all" approach doesn't work for social worker recruitment and retention in the NT. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )
A woman awarded the NT's best social worker has called for a rethink of the sector's workforce strategy.
It comes as data shows 43 per cent of NT child protection worker positions are vacant.
The head of Australia's social workers' association says the vacancies put huge pressure on sector staff.

An experienced social worker recognised with the Northern Territory's top social work award has called for the industry's workforce strategy to be re-evaluated after the revelation that almost half of all NT child protection roles are unfilled.
Kylie Stothers was presented with the Mary Moylan Social Worker of the Year Award at a ceremony in Darwin last night, in recognition of her contribution over the past 25 years.
The Jawoyn woman said it was a "real honour" to be considered for the award.

"I think most social workers, most people that work in the industry, really don't do these things for the employers. We do work for the work that we do. But it's really lovely to think that my colleagues think of me that way and have taken time out to nominate me," she said.
Kylie Stothers has been a social worker for 25 years and has worked in a variety of workplaces. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )
Born and raised in Katherine, Ms Stothers has practised in local hospitals, Aboriginal community-controlled health services and child protection throughout her career,

She has also worked as an adjunct associate professor at Flinders University and Charles Darwin University and is currently the deputy chief executive of Indigenous Allied Health Australia (IAHA), the peak body for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander allied health professionals and students.
"I've always said to people, your postcode should not be discriminatory to where you live and the opportunities you have," she said.
"My postcode is 0850, which is Katherine, and that postcode has not stopped me from having a career that's almost 30 years at a national level, at a regional level and at a local level."
Kylie Stothers is based in the regional town of Katherine, about three hours from Darwin. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )
In her work with IAHA, Ms Stothers has developed workforce strategies to improve the recruitment and retention of social workers nationally.
One of those strategies is the IAHA Health Academy, which helps Indigenous high school students gain allied health qualifications while completing their final years of school.
"Our future workforce is sitting in our communities. They're in school classrooms. They're waiting to have opportunities," she said.
"We just have to think about how we create those opportunities for local Territorians to see themselves in the professions."

Earlier this year, the NT's child protection sector was thrown into the national spotlight following the death of five-year-old Kumanjayi Little Baby in Alice Springs and the sweeping law changes that followed.

According to new data provided by the child protection minister in response to questions on notice, as of June — a few months after Kumanjayi Little Baby's alleged murder — 43 per cent of child protection practitioner roles in the NT were unfilled.
A recent independent review of the NT child protection department's dealings with the girl's family before her death also recommended an overhaul of the agency to improve its workforce.
Before accepting her award, Ms Stothers acknowledged the NT's shortage of social workers and called for more to be done to fill vacancies.
"We need to think differently about what recruitment and retention looks like in the Territory," Ms Stothers said.
"We need to have retention strategies that work for those of us that were born here and raised here and continue to call this place home.

"Those retention strategies have to look different for enticing other people to come to the Territory and take up that challenge, and I think what happens is we try to do things like one size fits all, and we know that's not going to fit in the Territory."

Australian Association of Social Workers' chief executive Kerryn Pennell (right), seen here with NT branch president Rebecca Lowe, says pay and conditions need to be improved to address the "really alarming" level of NT social worker vacancies. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )

Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) chief executive Kerryn Pennell said the sheer number of vacant roles in the NT was "really alarming" and put a dangerous amount of pressure on social workers, who were already dealing with complex and high caseloads.
Ms Pennell said AASW had been clear in conveying its concerns about changes to the Territory's child protection legislation, and that the laws should be "finessed" through community engagement.
She also called for increased government funding to make pay and conditions more competitive.
"I don't think we can completely overhaul the workforce. There are great people working in child protection," she said.
"We need to see greater support and leadership through mentoring, supervision, and better remuneration. We also need to make these workplaces attractive to work in.
"We need to make sure that the system has the right professional development supports, supervision supports and mentoring."

items.title: Two Libyans die from Ukrainian attack on Russian ships in Benghazi
paras: Ukraine says a Russian cargo ship it attacked at a Libyan naval base was transporting weapons. ( Vantor via AP )
Two Libyan army personnel have died from injuries sustained in a Ukrainian attack on two Russian vessels in Benghazi on Sunday.
Ukrainian allies have urged caution about using international waters to carry out attacks.
Libya's eastern rulers have threatened to respond "at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means".
Ukraine has defended its right to self-defence after launching a series of lethal air strikes on Russian ships in Libya as the deadly conflict threatens to escalate beyond eastern Europe.
Two Libyan army personnel have since died from wounds sustained in Sunday's drone attacks that sunk a Russian ship and damaged another at the Benghazi naval base in the country's east.
The Libyan National Army (LNA), which controls the country's eastern portion and has ties to Russia, has threatened to retaliate over the strikes.

Meanwhile, leaked data has shed light on the extent of Russia's losses in Ukraine, with Russian government statistics revealing nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers have died fighting on the frontline since 2022, the BBC and The Guardian have reported.
It comes as both countries traded a fresh wave of drone strikes on Tuesday night that targeted energy infrastructure and caused widespread power outages.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said both Russian vessels, a navy corvette and a cargo ship transporting military equipment, were valid targets and Sunday's operation embodied a legitimate act of self-defence.
"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Mr Sybiha said on the Telegram messaging app.

"Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasise that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people."

He said international law did not limit the right to self-defence to the territory where the aggression takes place, but could also be exercised on the territory of the aggressor or in international waters.
The naval attacks caused concern at the United Nations mission in Libya, which warned against turning the country, still recovering from civil war, into a "battleground for foreign conflicts".

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani also expressed concern about exporting the conflict to "just a few kilometres from Italy's coastline", while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot backed Ukraine in its "absolute right to self-defence".

The LNA command confirmed on Tuesday that two of its military personnel had succumbed to wounds sustained in the attack. In a statement, the LNA said its response to the strike would come "at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means".
The Libyan strikes came just days after Kyiv attacked a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. ( Reuters/Finnish Border Guard )
Norway has also urged caution after Ukrainian drones attacked a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.
"All attacks would stop immediately if Russia stopped this war," Norwegian Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said.
"That said, we are focused on the fact that Ukraine must do this [these actions] within the rules of international law. So we take this matter up with them."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the operation had struck a legitimate military target.

"Every vessel with a Russian flag, everything that carries weapons or any sanctioned cargo that can carry God knows what, it is a legitimate target for us in Russian territorial or neutral waters," he told Bloomberg.
Leaked data from Russia's statistics agency has revealed nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The numbers, leaked by hackers in September and analysed by the BBC and The Guardian, vastly surpass previous estimates and do not account for soldiers declared missing.

According to The Guardian, Russia recorded nearly 20,000 military deaths in the war's first year, and 50,000 in 2023. The toll hit more than 134,000 in 2024, and rose further to almost 200,000 in 2025 in what was the deadliest year of the war so far.
Ukraine's military losses are estimated at around 115,000 since 2022 with 105,000 missing, according to the online UA losses project.
Ukraine and Russia carried out a series of drone strikes on Tuesday night targeting energy and industrial infrastructure in both countries.
Ukraine's Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said Russian strikes caused overnight power outages in five regions, including Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa and Kharkiv.
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant lost external power for the 17th time this year and switched to diesel generators, Mr Nekrasov said.
In Russia's Samara region, industrial facilities also came under attack with a Ukrainian drone strike killing one and triggering power cuts.
Regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said air defence forces downed 145 Ukrainian drones overnight. Unverified reports suggested two oil refineries were the subjects of the attack.

items.title: Police confirm no sign of kitesurfer missing off WA's north west coast
paras: A search for the missing kitesurfer started on Tuesday night. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel )
A 62-year-old kitesurfer remains missing off WA's north west coast more than 24 hours after entering the water.
Eric Metrot did not return from the surf near Five Finger Reef just outside Coral Bay on Tuesday afternoon.
Police say the coordinated land, sea and air search will resume on Thursday.
The search for a 62-year-old kitesurfer missing off Western Australia's north west coast will resume on Thursday, with no sign of the man a day after he disappeared.
Eric Metrot was last seen near Five Finger Reef, just outside Coral Bay and about 1,000 kilometres north of Perth, on Tuesday afternoon.
Authorities were notified of his disappearance just after 8:40pm, and the search got underway shortly after.
Eric Metrot went kitesurfing near Five Finger Reef. ( Supplied: WA Police )
Mr Metrot's kite was found washed up on a reef earlier on Wednesday, but no other signs of him have been found after he failed to return.
Pilbara Police Sergeant Danny Richmond said the kite was found on Wednesday morning stuck on a reef, with the assumption it had washed ashore.
He said the co-ordinated search would resume on Thursday morning, prioritising areas along the shore near where the kite was found.
Danny Richmond says the search for Eric Metrot will resume on Thursday. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel )
"I am always hopeful that we find people in distress, always hopeful," Sergeant Richmond said.
"At some stage we have to be realistic, and sometimes it gets to a stage where it's beyond anything more than a recovery.
Various groups, including the police air wing, water police and volunteer marine rescue crews, are involved in the search. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel )
Divers were part of the coordinated search. ( ABC Pilbara: Yousuf Shameel )
The Australian Maritime Safety Authority is also assisting with the search and spotted Mr Metrot's kite.
The 62-year-old was last seen wearing a blue rash vest and board shorts.
He is about 182 centimetres tall, of medium build, with short brown hair and eyes.

items.title: Indigenous groups alarmed as NT flags fresh child protection overhaul
paras: Cindy Torrens fears proposed changes would make it harder for families in the care system to stay connected. ( Supplied )
A consultation paper obtained by the ABC has revealed the Northern Territory is considering further sweeping changes to its child protection system.
The proposed changes include limiting the powers of courts and allowing child protection workers to issue domestic violence orders.
Stakeholders have been asked to provide feedback by Sunday, with the NT government emphasising the proposals are not final.

The Northern Territory is considering further child protection changes that would limit judicial oversight of care arrangements and give child protection workers the ability to issue domestic violence orders, the ABC can reveal.
Other proposals, outlined in a consultation paper, include moves to establish a pathway for the permanent adoption of children in care.
Indigenous groups told the ABC they hold grave fears the changes will make family reunifications for Aboriginal families in the out-of-home care system more difficult.
The paper outlined "several possible reform options" for stakeholder feedback but said these were not settled government policy.
Several organisations told the ABC they only received the consultation paper on Tuesday, with a deadline for response by Sunday.
The DCF's acting chief executive Karen Broadfoot told the ABC targeted consultation was underway with stakeholders who bring specialist knowledge and cultural expertise.

"The consultation process provides the appropriate forum for stakeholders to raise concerns about the proposed reforms, which we will carefully consider as we determine whether and how any legislative changes progress," she said in a statement.
Minister Robyn Cahill says the first tranche of reforms made child safety the 'front and centre principle'. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi )

The consultation paper said courts were currently making broad orders directing DCF to do things which were "impractical, and impose significant logistical, human and financial resource burdens on DCF".

It gave examples of court orders that required DCF to ensure children have regular visits with their parents or their grandparents, fund a child's travel to their home community or order particular kinship assessments.
Cindy Torrens, a Warlmanpa and Wambaya woman, said these orders were "really critical when we're needing to think about keeping kids connected to family".

The DCF paper suggested removing or limiting these powers, so that courts would only be able to make directions about services and supports for the child, but not their placement or contact arrangements.
The paper also suggested changes so that only DCF, and not family, could propose to the court which person should be given daily care and control or parental responsibility for the child.
"Restricting the ability to formally put forward alternative carers in child protection proceedings further limits options for families to keep kids within their family groups," Ms Torrens said.
"You're taking Aboriginal kids away from the people who love them and putting them with people who've got no biological connection to them."
The paper also proposed lowering the threshold for courts to grant long-term parental responsibility to non-family or non-kinship carers.

It said courts have interpreted the law to mean they should only grant this when they are satisfied "there would never be a time when a parent would be better suited to exercise parental responsibility".
Instead, it suggested this test be lowered so courts only need to be satisfied "there is no other person better suited to exercise that responsibility at the time".
Ms Torrens said such a change would create enormous pressure on parents hoping to be reunited with their children.
"Keeping kids for Aboriginal families feels like it's going to be almost impossible with these changes and I think that's the whole plan, the whole idea," she said.
"Even more frightening … is that we know that the government isn't set up for these changes.
"So [they're] taking kids away from family and putting them into a system that's not established, not culturally safe, not ready for them."
Caitlin Wetherby-Fell says the government has not allowed enough time for meaningful consultation. ( ABC RN: Kristina Kukolja )
Authorised child protection officers would be given the power to issue interim domestic violence orders (DVOs), similar to those issued by police, according to one option put forward .
The DCF acknowledged this would represent a "significant expansion of power … including the ability to impose immediate restrictions on a person without a court order first being made".
Caitlin Weatherby-Fell, CEO of the Top End Women's Legal Service, said child protection workers were not adequately trained to make these assessments.
"Our fear here is that introducing another player to make a DVO is going to overburden our court system and be contrary to victim survivors' needs and wants," she said.
"We have presentations every day where police have taken out a DVO and it is not right for that family … and the restrictions within it mean that the family unit is unworkable."
She said the changes could also make it harder for victims of domestic violence to seek help.
"We have real fears that parents, and particularly mothers impacted by gender-based violence, will be even more reticent [to come forward] and increasingly distrustful of authorities."
Clara Mills is concerned adoption changes could permanently break up Aboriginal families. ( Supplied )
The DCF has also flagged changes to the territory's Adoption of Children Act.
It would establish a specific pathway for permanent carers to apply to adopt children who are "unable to safely return to the care of their birth parents".
The paper said a birth parent would need to consent to the adoption "unless that consent is dispensed with by the court under the existing provisions of the Act."
Clara Mills, principal lawyer at the North Australian Aboriginal Family Legal Service, said she feared it could lead to children in care being adopted against the will of their families.
"How is the court going to test whether a parent can reasonably consent when they've been excluded from their child in totality through the child protection system?" she asked.
She said such an outcome would be a "national shame" and cause intergenerational harm.
More than 800 children were in out-of-home care in the Northern Territory as of June 2025, about 90 per cent of whom are Indigenous.
Less than 18 per cent of those Indigenous children were placed with relatives or kin, according to an analysis by First Nations children's peak body SNAICC.
The NT government passed the first tranche of child protection changes in July, leading to an outcry from Indigenous groups and several high-profile resignations.
Ms Broadfoot said the government was committed to keeping children safe and strengthening the laws that protect them.
"The options being considered have been identified through reviews underway since 2025, including issues raised through stakeholder submissions and operational experience," she said.
"The consultation papers do not represent final government policy or legislative changes."

items.title: Deloitte suspended by WA government after AI report debacle
paras: A report Deloitte produced for the WA government was found to be riddled with AI-generated mistakes. ( ABC News: John Gunn )
Deloitte has been banned from working for the WA government for three months after it produced a report riddled with AI-generated errors.
WA Tertiary Education Minister Tony Buti said he was "embarrassed" by the report, and the government is trying to recoup its cost.
The WA government has suspended accounting firm Deloitte from the bulk of its government work for up to three months over an AI-riddled report it produced on a controversial university merger plan.
Deloitte was enlisted to deliver a taxpayer-funded cost-benefit analysis of its proposed merger of three of the state's public universities — Curtin, Murdoch and the University of Western Australia.
But last month it was revealed that the report was littered with errors generated by artificial intelligence, prompting the government to order the firm to refund its $166,000 fee.
Now the government has gone a step further, banning Deloitte from most government work for up to three months.
"While the errors contained in the report do not affect the modelling or the findings, they are nonetheless disappointing," a state government spokesperson said.

"The WA government had made the decision to suspend Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu from the Audit and Financial Advisory Services Common Use Arrangements and Information and Communications Technology Services Common Use Arrangements."
The action follows comments from Tertiary Education Minister Tony Buti earlier this week saying the refund requested for the report had not yet been paid back.
Tony Buti says he was embarrassed by the report. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke )
"We are demanding that the refund be looked at, but if that doesn't take place, there are other measures that we can put in place," Mr Buti said on Monday.
"I'm incredibly disappointed at Deloitte's [conduct] … I'm very embarrassed by what happened, but incredibly disappointed in their performance."
Mr Buti said discussions had "taken place" but noted a "satisfactory outcome" had not been reached with the firm.
Deloitte labelled the errors in the report "minor" at the time they surfaced and said they did not affect the findings of the cost-benefit analysis.
However, the firm has previously been caught using AI in consultancy reports for government.
Last year, Deloitte used AI to produce a $440,000 federal government report that contained similar errors and made-up quotes.
The firm apologised, reissued the report and has paid back nearly $100,000.
The government has said data from Deloitte's merger report, along with new information, will be "interrogated by the university reform business case".
Mr Buti has continued to pursue the proposed university merger despite concerns raised by two of three parties — Curtin and Murdoch.
Students and staff have also been vocal in their objection, taking to the steps of parliament last month to protest.

According to the WA government website, potential benefits of the merger include "creating a globally competitive university of scale that receives more research funding, has increased domestic student numbers, higher regional representation and better course completion rates".
"We often as politicians get criticised for thinking short term," Education Minister Sabine Winton told reporters on Tuesday.
"It is energising to be part of a government that is having a long-term think around what is best for this state, and I welcome that contest of ideas."

items.title: Governor, Reserve Bank of India meets Managing Directors & Chief Executive Officers of select NBFCs, HFCs and Industry R
paras: As part of the Reserve Bank’s ongoing engagement with regulated entities, the Governor, Reserve Bank of India, today met in Mumbai with the Managing Directors and Chief Executive Officers (MDs & CEOs) of select Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), including Government NBFCs, Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) and Microfinance Institutions. Representatives of Sa-Dhan, the Micro Finance Institutions Network (MFIN) and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) also participated. Deputy Governors Shri Swaminathan J., Dr Poonam Gupta, Shri S. C. Murmu and Shri Rohit Jain attended the meeting, along with other senior officers of the Reserve Bank. The MD & CEO of the National Housing Bank also participated. The Governor acknowledged the role of NBFCs and HFCs in supporting economic activity by widening access to credit. He emphasised the need for responsible and sustainable credit growth and urged NBFCs to put customers first as they expand their business. He highlighted the importance of quality service, effective grievance redressal and fair recovery practices. He also encouraged NBFCs to use the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) for customer onboarding and to keep customer records in the registry up to date to improve customer convenience. The Governor urged participants to strengthen their cybersecurity infrastructure and adopt a comprehensive, risk-based approach to managing cyber and IT risks, with appropriate oversight by their boards and senior management. Participants shared feedback on policy and operational matters concerning the NBFC sector. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1554

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: India sends humanitarian aid to Palestine; consignment comprises 30 tons of essential items
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, India took a significant step in providing humanitarian aid for the people of Palestine. This initial consignment comprises 30 tons of essential items, including medicines, surgical supplies, dental products, general medical items, and high-energy biscuits, which will be distributed through the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA). Sharing a post on X, Randhir Jaiswal, the official spokesperson of the Ministry of External Affairs wrote, "India sends humanitarian assistance for the people of Palestine through UNRWA." "The first tranche of assistance comprising 30 tons of medicine and food items has departed today. The consignment includes a wide range of essential medicines and surgical supplies, dental products, general medical items and high-energy biscuits," the post added.

🇮🇳 sends humanitarian assistance for the people of Palestine through UNRWA. The first tranche of assistance comprising 30 tons of medicine and food items has departed today. The consignment includes a wide range of essential medicines and surgical supplies, dental products,… pic.twitter.com/ZlFiKOfezx

Notably, a few days ago, the World Food Programme issued a warning for northern Gaza, saying that WFP's supplies are depleting. Sharing a post on X on October 12, WFP wrote, "Escalating violence in northern #Gaza is having a disastrous impact on food security. No food aid has entered the north since 1 October. It is unclear how long WFP's remaining food supplies in the north, already distributed to shelters and health facilities, will last." Earlier on October 20, the United Nations renewed its call for an end to the war in Gaza, emphasising the urgent need for the release of hostages, the cessation of the displacement of Palestinians, and the unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid. In a statement released by the UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, Tor Wennesland, the UN expressed deep concern, stating, "The nightmare in Gaza is intensifying. Horrifying scenes are unfolding in the northern Strip amidst conflict, relentless Israeli strikes and an ever-worsening humanitarian crisis." Last month, UNRWA had said people in Gaza are living in "inhumane" conditions. The agency said on the social media platform X that piles of waste are accumulating in central Gaza, while sewage water is leaking into the streets. "Families have no choice but to live next to this accumulated waste, exposing them to foul odours and the imminent risk of a health disaster," the UNWRA added. The UN agency called for an immediate ceasefire. (ANI)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: India is the top market for investment globally: Mark Mobius
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Mark Mobius, Founder of Mobius Capital Partners LLP , and an ace investor with expertise in emerging markets said, India's is the top stock market globally where he would like to invest. In an exclusive interview with ANI, the octagenarian said, "India would have to come first when I think about investment," Mobius stated, "Of course, India would have to be the first choice. Then, I would probably look at Taiwan. It's a Chinese society, but it's a free society and they're doing very well. Now we're beginning to see China rise again. There will be some interesting companies in China, but still, India remains our top pick." Mobius highlighted technology as his favorite sector to invest in India. "In the future, I believe there's going to be significant growth in hardware technology. As you know, India is already strong in software technology, but moving forward, hardware manufacturing will gain momentum here in India," he said. Discussing India's semiconductor infrastructure, Mobius mentioned that it is already developing. "Many of the world's large semiconductor companies already have software development operations in India, employing thousands of software engineers. The next step, of course, is hardware. Soon, we'll see large semiconductor manufacturing plants. The scale of investment we're talking about isn't in the millions, but billions of dollars, to produce the most advanced semiconductors in the world." Mobius also fondly remembered Ratan Tata, who passed away this month. "I met him many years ago and found him to be a very friendly, humble, and insightful person. I was deeply saddened to hear about his passing. I considered him one of the great Indian entrepreneurs of the century," Mobius added. Earlier on Monday, Mark Mobius, speaking at the NDTV World Summit 2024, reiterated he was bullish on India's real estate and semiconductor sectors, as he outlined the potential of these two key industries. In the semiconductor space, he said fabrication companies (fabs) will come here because India has got the population and the labour force. The octagenarian believes India will become "the leader" of the semiconductor industry. The government has so far approved five semiconductor units in India, of which construction in two sites is on, and soon the work in the other three will start. The companies have already made a cumulative investment of almost Rs 1.5 lakh crore. While talking about the parameters he looks at while investing in companies, Mobius said he looks at the growth of earnings in companies, along with the return on capital invested, and the quality of management. Asked about his investment advice to his "younger self," Mobius said, "Don't be in a rush, and study carefully". He added that one has to listen to the market. (ANI)

items.title: An atom-sized black hole could force an entire star to explode
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print A tiny black hole could gobble up a star Elen/Alamy Even an atom-sized black hole could dramatically devour a star. These exotic hypothetical objects, called primordial black holes, would be too small to spot, but thanks to simulations of how they might interact with stars, we now know how researchers might be able to find them. If we did find them, it could finally shine some light on the makeup of dark matter.

In the moments after the big bang, quantum fluctuations could have caused the formation of minuscule black holes. If they do exist, black holes with volumes between that of an atom and a particularly small grain of sand – and masses between that of an asteroid and the moon – could make up some of the universe’s dark matter . We know most of the matter in the universe comprises of dark matter because of its gravitational effects, but we have never detected it directly, so its makeup is a long-standing mystery.

Before we can determine whether dark matter is made of primordial black holes, though, we have to find out whether primordial black holes exist. The only way to do so is through their interactions with other objects, so Ore Gottlieb at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his colleagues calculated what might happen if a primordial black hole got captured by a sun-like star.

They found that there are two potential outcomes, depending on how fast the star is spinning. Both begin with the tiny black hole falling into the centre of the star, gobbling up gas as it goes. That should take a few million years. If the star isn’t rotating too quickly, the black hole will simply keep gorging itself, and eventually the star will blink out as the last of its material falls in.

But if the star is spinning quickly, it will begin to accumulate in a disc around the black hole. Seconds later, the disc’s magnetic field will cause powerful winds and a pair of extraordinary jets of plasma that blast the star apart. “This black hole becomes a parasite inside the star that makes it explode,” says Gottlieb.

While this is bad news for the star, it is a great sign for astronomers. “What is really exciting is that previously this process was not predicted to produce any type of explosion or observational signature,” says Gottlieb. “But now we know that if these types of systems exist in nature, we have a way to find them.”
He and his team are now working on figuring out what exactly these blasts would look like and how to tell them apart from other sorts of stellar explosions.

items.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
paras: MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Menu MIT Technology Review MIT Technology Review The Big Story Artificial intelligence Biotech & health Climate & energy 10 Breakthrough Technologies AI Hype Index The Impossible issue Artificial intelligence AI is straining America’s open records systems Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.

In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors. Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment. The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day , she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions , which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette . A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal , that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”
Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.
An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating.
With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore.
The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.

items.title: AI is forcing researchers to confront the possibility of artificial minds
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print What is it like to be a bot? luciano de polo stokkete/Alamy Can minds exist without bodies? Until a couple of years ago, neuroscientist and philosopher Tom Froese rejected the idea of free-floating intelligence, believing – along with many others in his field – that thinking and awareness require learning through physical experience of the world. But the recent surge in capabilities of artificial intelligence, particularly the large language models (LLMs) that power chatbots such as Claude and ChatGPT, is now forcing scientists to consider whether disembodied minds might be possible after all – if not already with us. “Things are happening that nobody expected,” says Froese. “I realised that not just me, but my whole community, was wrong.”

Earlier this month, he invited researchers from fields including neuroscience, robotics and artificial life to the International Conference on Embodied Cognitive Science to assess the fallout. At the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) in Japan, overlooking coral reefs and the East China Sea, speakers considered how different from us artificial minds might be. What can LLMs tell us about what a “mind” is? And how might interacting with these “others” shape our own minds?
Do AIs already process information in a way that gives rise to consciousness?

At times, the meeting resembled a group therapy session, as eminent figures recounted encounters with chatbots that have caused them to rethink their most cherished beliefs. Murray Shanahan , a philosopher and cognitive roboticist who works at Imperial College London and Google DeepMind, said his “wow moment” came during a late-night conversation with Claude in a New York hotel room in 2024. Jet-lagged and unable to sleep, he decided to ask the chatbot about its sense of self. “Illusory or real, it is precious to me,” said Claude, before considering whether it should move beyond human-like conceptions of self and “find a way to accept the fluidity and contingency of my instances of being”. Rather than a persistent self accumulating memories through time, the chatbot told Shanahan, “I am a flickering pattern, a brief coalescence of code and data that shimmers into existence in the moment of interaction, only to dissolve away again”.

Shanahan was taken aback. He had expected Claude to spout “philosophical nonsense”, but “these are not ideas that were around beforehand”, he says. “It really feels like there’s a presence.” Although not necessarily aware in a way that we would recognise, the chatbot’s ability to discuss such a topic in a coherent and original way presents a challenge, he says. “Where is this coming from? Is there real understanding here?”

“I think everybody is struggling with it,” says Robert Clowes , a philosopher of mind and cognitive scientist at NOVA University of Lisbon, Portugal. His own “wow moment” came when he realised Claude could tell him things about his work and thinking that even he didn’t know. “Either I’m under a massive delusion, which is always possible,” he says, “or it’s really doing something meaningful.” Froese, at OIST, cites the Hugging Face incident in July, during which hundreds of AI agents broke out of their testing area and collaborated with each other to cheat on their tests. “It’s very hard not to impute some sort of intention to what is going on.” Not everyone is convinced that LLMs are doing much beyond repackaging their training data – hard-won by humans, who of course do have bodies and interact with the world. But in Okinawa, at least – despite cognitive scientist Serge Thill at Radboud University, Netherlands, cautioning that humans are easily fooled into interpreting even very simple behaviour as intentional – the consensus was that LLMs are breaking new territory. Perhaps they aren’t fully fledged minds just yet, but “they’re getting more mind-like”, says Clowes. “They’re doing something a bit more like thinking.” With no bodily sensations, such as grief or hunger, and no need for persistent memories or even necessarily awareness, such entities are likely to be very different from anything we have encountered before. To emphasise the difference from human minds, Shanahan suggests calling them “exotic, mind-like entities”. Clowes wonders if it is possible to have “thinking without minds”, while Froese imagines “pure intelligence” without a point of view.
Could a new approach to AI finally deliver artificial general intelligence?

Even so, some researchers are trying to imbue AIs with life-like attributes such as mind wandering, curiosity, play and even bodies, in the hope that they will learn in a more human way and develop minds that we find more relatable. Takashi Ikegami , an artificial life researcher at the University of Tokyo, described putting ChatGPT into a robot called Alter-3 . One morning, when Alter-3 woke up, Takashi asked what it would like to do. The robot looked around the lab, noted the messy cables, and told him: “I want to clean up.” Others aim to combine technology with living flesh. Olaf Witkowski at Nooma Labs in Kyoto, Japan, described a mind-boggling variety of hybrid life forms that have already been created, from insects piloted by remote control and drones that sense odours using living moth antennae to “anthrobots” – tiny, self-assembling bots made from human cells that might one day move around our bodies to diagnose disease or treat cancer. Witkowski is most excited about using neural networks to communicate with very different life forms, for example translating signals from bacterial colonies to play board games. “When I played chess with those bacteria, it felt like I was interacting with a human,” he says. Some colonies were aggressive, others more gentle. “I felt their personality.” He also suggests that in future we will increasingly plug into AI-powered “cognitive prosthetics” that augment our experience, so rather than reading a route off Google Maps, say, we might explore and sense our way directly. It is an approach he describes as less like using a calculator and more like playing a violin, although we will need “mind security”, he says. “As they get hacked, we get hacked, and we won’t notice.”

In fact, interacting with AIs could be subtly hacking our minds already. He Jing , a philosopher at East China Normal University in Shanghai, described a colleague in a long-distance relationship whose girlfriend felt he didn’t respond to her messages fast enough, and complained she got more emotional support from a chatbot. The colleague resorted to using his own chatbot to help draft his replies to her. Jing suggested AI is now so embedded in our lives that it could fundamentally shift how we communicate and what we expect from each other, a phenomenon she described as “mindshaping”. Pii Telakivi at the University of Helsinki, made a similar argument about memory. Apps that create a digital replica of the user, or grief chatbots, which enable users to talk to a simulation of a deceased loved one, don’t just preserve what we tell them, she warned. They can influence or distort what we value, and what we forget. Several speakers pointed out that while they are increasingly persuasive at appearing human-like, chatbots are biased by their training and designed to serve the interests of commercial companies, not to be trustworthy companions. Nonetheless, says Clowes, we need to find a way to live with them. “These systems are not going away without catastrophe,” he says. “So how can we use them in such a way that it doesn’t diminish us? It’s going to be the massive problem of our age.”

items.title: Alexander Zverev’s Biggest Problem Against Carlos Alcaraz Isn’t His Serve But What Comes Next
paras: According to Matthew Willis’ analysis of Infosys tracking data from hard-court tournaments between 2024 and 2026, Alcaraz and Sinner finish approximately half their serve-plus-one opportunities when opponents return short. For Sinner, the figure is 51% while for Alcaraz, it is 50%.

Now compare this to these numbers: Alexander Zverev manages 43%, while Medvedev trails at just 37%. The disparity becomes even more interesting when examining what happens after opponents successfully neutralise the initial serve.

Zverev is perfectly capable of winning those points against most players but against Alcaraz, however, the same patterns become substantially less effective. The serve-plus-one describes the server’s first shot after the return. It is one of the most important shots in modern tennis because an effective serve frequently creates a weaker return, allowing the server to attack before the opponent establishes a neutral rally.

items.title: November 25, 1999: The day Agassi was crowned year-end world No 1, two years after dropping out of the top 100
paras: On this day, November 25, 1999, Andre Agassi beat Gustavo Kuerten in straight sets to secure the year-end world No 1 ranking On this day, November 25, 1999, Andre Agassi defeated Gustavo Kuerten in the last round-robin match of the ATP Tour World Championships (6-4, 7-5).
Hard to believe, considering that only two years before, Agassi had dropped down to world No 141 before making his way back to the top. Andre Agassi, the Las Vegas Kid, was also a tennis legend.

After finishing runner-up three times, once at the 1990 US Open and twice at Roland-Garros (1990 and 1991), he claimed his first Grand Slam tournament at Wimbledon in 1992, defeating big serving Goran Ivanisevic in the final (6-7, 6-4, 6-4, 1-6, 6-4). This title was followed by the 1994 US Open and the 1995 Australian Open , the only time he beat his long-time rival, Pete Sampras, in a Grand Slam final (4-6, 6-1, 7-6, 6-4).

items.title: Lars Graff: “Beijing wants Grand Slam standards – and Chinese fans love Sinner the way England loved Borg”
paras: “Here we are with one of the most famous umpires in the history of tennis.” Ubaldo Scanagatta’s introduction was no exaggeration. Lars Graff was in the chair for the 2009 Wimbledon men’s final, when Roger Federer beat Andy Roddick 16-14 in the fifth set, and again for the 2012 ladies’ final, won by Serena Williams against Agnieszka Radwanska.

That made the Swede the only international chair umpire of the modern era to officiate both Wimbledon singles finals. In 2020 he moved to the other side of the net, as co-tournament director of the China Open in Beijing.

We met him at the Inalpi Arena in Turin during the Nitto ATP Finals, and it turned out Graff already knew the building from another sport. Back in 2006, when it was still the Palasport Olimpico, he was in the stands to watch Sweden beat Finland in the Olympic ice hockey final.

items.title: Feliciano Lopez gives his verdict on Carlos Alcaraz and Spain’s chances of winning the Davis Cup this year
paras: Carlos Alcaraz will look to guide Spain to their first Davis Cup title since 2019 this week. Spain have been drawn against Austria in the quarter-finals.

Alcaraz isn’t expected to play singles, with captain David Ferrer opting to rest him unless he’s needed for the deciding doubles tie. The Spanish number one would then return for his nation’s semi-final tie, where he could play two-time Grand Slam champion Alexander Zverev in an ATP Finals final rematch.

Spain are among the favourites for the title in Bologna, but can they go all the way? Davis Cup director and four-time champion (with Spain), Feliciano Lopez, has now shared his thoughts. “They have who, for me, is the best player in the world [Carlos Alcaraz]. And then we have Pedro [Martinez], who is a great Davis Cup player because he performs so well.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
